title: The name he called
hook: Ajamila, dying and afraid, calls his son Narayana and Vishnu's messengers come; why puja begins with a call, and the bell sounds it
carry: the bell is a call: come

segments.voice: Yesterday, pushpa, and Vishnu ready to give his own eye. Your line was the flower stands for your heart. Today, the small thing with a handle, and a man who called a name.
screen: `PUSHPA — THE FLOWER STANDS FOR YOUR HEART.`

segments.voice: Ajamila started out as a good young man who kept every rule. Then he fell for the wrong life, left his wife, and lived for decades by cheating and stealing. He had ten children, and he adored the youngest, a little boy named Narayana, one of Vishnu's names. At eighty-eight, Ajamila lay dying, and he saw them coming: three terrifying messengers of Death, ropes in their hands. He panicked, and did what a frightened father does. He shouted for his little boy, playing outside. Narayana! He wasn't praying. He was just calling his son.
screen: `A GOOD MAN WHO WENT WRONG.` → `HIS YOUNGEST SON: NARAYANA.` → `DEATH'S MESSENGERS ARRIVE.` → `HE CALLS THE NAME.`

segments.voice: But the name he called was God's. And in the Bhagavata Purana, the moment it leaves his mouth, Vishnu's own messengers appear and stop Death's messengers cold. They argue it out, and Vishnu's side wins: a name of God, called even by accident, even half-meant, is heard. Ajamila is released, and he spends the rest of his life in prayer. Some families say that's one reason so many Hindu children carry God's names: every time you call them, you've called God too. Now, the bell. Its Sanskrit name is ghanta. Every puja begins with a call, called avahana: inviting God to come. And the bell is the sound of that call. Many families say a short traditional verse as they ring it, asking the gods to come and anything in the way to go. So the bell isn't an alarm clock for a sleepy God. It's a call, made by someone who trusts, like the story does, that calling is enough to be heard. That's why it rings at the very start of puja, again through arti, and why people ring the big bell at a temple door as they walk in. On top of many hand bells sits a little figure: Garuda, the eagle who carries Vishnu, or Nandi, Shiva's bull. Many teachers add a second reading: the bell calls you too. By the time its long ring fades, you're here.
screen: `VISHNU'S MESSENGERS STOP DEATH'S.` · `GHANTA: PUJA BEGINS WITH A CALL.` · `NOT AN ALARM CLOCK. A CALL.` · `THE BELL CALLS YOU TOO.`

segments.voice: Strike a bell once, gently, or a glass with a spoon, or just imagine the sound. If you pray, let the ring be your call, and say one name you honor, Narayana, Krishna, Shiva, Ma, quietly, once. Then don't move. Follow the sound as it thins out, until you can't tell whether you still hear it. When it's gone, notice where you are. You were called too.
Ghanta. The bell: rung at the start of puja to call God in, the sound of a call that, the story says, is always heard.
Your line: the bell is a call: come. Ajamila only called his son's name, and it was enough. Day one hundred fourteen, done.

screen: `THE BELL IS A CALL: COME.` → `DAY 114 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE RIVER THAT CAME DOWN.`

howItsDone: Many Hindus ring a small hand bell at the start of puja as part of inviting the deity (avahana), often saying a short traditional verse, ring it again during arti, and ring the large bell at a temple's entrance as they walk in. Many hand bells carry a figure on the handle, often Garuda for Vishnu's devotees or Nandi for Shiva's.

what a scholar hears: avahana (invocation) is among the first of the classic sixteen services of puja; a traditional verse said while ringing the ghanta asks the gods to come and obstructing forces to go; Ajamila's story (Bhagavata Purana 6.1-2) is the classic teaching on the power of the divine name, even said indirectly.
